/* The night sky the dark shells paint behind their content: a core, a middle and an edge, read
   * outward from the top of the page. Two features drew it from the same three literals — the
   * marketplace's agent routes and /apply — which is a ground the product depends on and had never
   * named. The edge is load-bearing beyond the gradient: eight scrims in apply and markets are the
   * same colour at a fraction, so a change to it that reached only the gradient would leave the
   * scrims behind. They now read it through the triple below rather than retyping it.
   *
   * These sit here rather than under the dark surface for the reason the agent fills do: a scene
   * does not become a different scene because the page around it changed. Nothing paints them on
   * light — both `.space` elements render only when their shell is dark. */
  --pk-space-core: #1b1f6b;
  --pk-space-mid: #0a0b2e;
  --pk-space-edge: #05061a;

  /* The edge again, as an `r, g, b` triple, because the eight scrims above could not be written
   * from `--pk-space-edge`: rgba() will not take a custom property for its first three arguments.
   * That is the same constraint `accentVars` documents for `--accent-rgb` and the same workaround,
   * so this applies a precedent rather than setting one. It is written down twice on purpose, and
   * a value that drifts apart shows up as a scrim that no longer matches the sky behind it.
   *
   * `color: var(--pk-space-edge-rgb)` is not a colour, so probe.mjs's sentinel excludes this from
   * the values tokens.mjs compares against. The triple makes the scrims track the palette; the two
   * veils below are what a check can recognise, because they hold the composited value and the
   * check keys on alpha as well as hue. */
  --pk-space-edge-rgb: 5, 6, 26;

  /* The edge as a scrim, at the two weights the scene can actually tell apart.
   *
   * There were five: 0.45, 0.5, 0.55 and 0.6 across seven places, plus a 0.4 in markets that turned
   * out not to belong to this scene at all. Nobody chose 0.45 over 0.5, and naming all five would
   * have made a drift permanent by giving it the look of a decision — a literal is obviously
   * unconsidered, a token is not.
   *
   * Two rather than three or one, decided by measuring rather than by eye. Every sky pixel /apply
   * paints was sampled — 1.36M of them, from #05061A out to the brightest point of the core — and
   * each alpha composited against every one. Adjacent fifths of an alpha differ by at most dE 1.9
   * to 2.1, under the ~2.3 just-noticeable threshold, so 0.45 folds into 0.5 and 0.55 into 0.6 with
   * nothing visible moving. The two that remain differ by dE 4.05, which is above it, so both names
   * are earned. One weight was tested and refused: it lands 3.87 from the far end, which is a
   * difference somebody could point at.
   *
   * Why these are colours and not an `opacity`, when .trailLine took the opposite route: that line
   * IS the thing being painted and has no children, so weighting the element weights only it. A
   * scrim sits *under* content — fading .header would fade the brand and the nav with it. */
  --pk-space-veil: rgba(var(--pk-space-edge-rgb), 0.5);
  --pk-space-veil-strong: rgba(var(--pk-space-edge-rgb), 0.6);

/* The rim a lit element carries: a bright hairline on a saturated fill against the night sky.
   * Three places wanted it — the glow button below, and the two accent pixels in /apply — and all
   * three had typed the same value, which is agreement by coincidence rather than by contract.
   *
   * Not `--pk-border-strong`, which is 0.32 on dark and deliberately quieter: the edge of a panel
   * and the rim of something lit are different questions, and answering one with the other is what
   * makes a rim look like a border. */
